item.description:
URL: https://www.experimental-history.com/p/we-need-more-goat-sacrifices, See on Hacker News

Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLD, I’d like to send you a little something extra in the mail. Submit your preorder receipt and your mailing address here. This is only available to folks with US or UK addresses—apologies to those who live elsewhere! In the US, everyone with a valid entry will get one; in the UK they’ll pick winners randomly. The link will be open until December 11, and we’ll start mailing things out after that. I won’t spoil the surprise, but I will say that a) it’s very silly, and b) I can’t wait to get mine.

(For the US: US Residents, 18+. Ends December 11, 2026. See terms at https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder)

Anyway, onto the post!

Before anybody enacts a major social policy or launches any philanthropic programs, they should sacrifice a goat. There ought to be an entire liturgy of grotesqueries, in fact—pricked fingers, names written in blood, robes, candles, chanting, obsidian blades, still-beating hearts, the whole shebang.

The point of this ritual is not to signal our obeisance to the gods (although if any of them want to stop by and help us out, that would be cool), but to remind ourselves that we know nothing. This is procedurally-induced humility, which is desperately necessary, because an alarming number of our best-intentioned interventions do not work.

For example:

  • In 2009, Congress spent $3 billion on “School Improvement Grants” for the worst-performing schools in the country. As far as we can tell, those grants did nothing.

  • Universities that hired a Chief Diversity Officer between 2001 and 2019 did not end up with more diverse students, faculties, or administrators.

  • The American government spent $280 million to help Afghan women get jobs, and now they can’t really say whether any women got any jobs.1

  • Remember 20 years ago, when giving laptops to kids in developing countries seemed like the most important thing to do? Well, a 10-year RCT of 531 rural schools in Peru found zero effects of “One Laptop Per Child” on academic performance.2

  • Researchers developed four different messages that were supposed to convince parents to vaccinate their kids. None of the messages worked, and one of them accidentally made parents more likely to believe that vaccines cause autism.

Most of those are left-coded failures, so here are some right-coded failures:

  • When Arkansas added a work requirement to Medicaid, the number of Arkansans with health insurance went down without any increase in employment.

  • In 2002, the Bush administration launched the Building Strong Families Program, which provided counseling to low-income, unmarried parents with the goal of strengthening their relationships, keeping them both in their child’s life, and ultimately getting them married. Three years later, an independent evaluation found that the program did none of those things.

  • And here is the effect of four different abstinence-only sex ed programs that run across the United States:

In the social sciences, nothing ever dies; it merely becomes embarrassing. We can’t say that it’s impossible for anything like these programs to ever succeed, given enough time, flimsy theorizing, and generous definitions of “success”. The point is that these effects should be large, and instead they are nonexistent. Seems to me like it’s time to get the goats in here.

It’s inevitable that some of our interventions are going to fail. (If they don’t, we should either be suspicious of the results, or we should be more ambitious with our programs.) What we really want to know is: when we try to improve the world through some policy or program, how often do we succeed?

We don’t have a good answer to this question, but we do have a good joke about it.

In 1987, the sociologist Peter Rossi wrote a tongue-in-cheek paper that accidentally became his intellectual legacy. He would later refer to it as “far from being one of my favorites” and “the source of considerable embarrassment”, and yet it’s the only thing of his that I’ve ever read or even heard of.3 It was called “The Iron Law of Evaluation and Other Metallic Rules“, and it went like this, lightly paraphrased:

  • The Iron Law of Evaluation: The net expected impact of a large social program is zero.

  • The Stainless Steel Law: Better-designed evaluations are more likely to find null effects.

  • The Brass Law: The more a program is intended to change people, the more likely the impact of that program will be zero.

  • The Zinc Law: The programs most likely to be evaluated are those most likely to fail.

Rossi tried to walk back his laws shortly before he died in 2006, insisting that there is now a “large number of well conducted impact assessments that yield statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”. Still, even after supposedly enduring 16 years of embarrassment from his one satirical paper, he concluded, “we really do not know whether programs over a wide variety of substantive areas are worth anything”.

Rossi did not do us the favor of actually naming any of those “statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”, and I know why, because I have gone looking for them, and they are not easy to find. The Earned Income Tax Credit, which is designed to benefit low- and middle-income families, was once considered a slam dunk; now a new analysis suggests that it might not do anything. Plain packaging—where you strip cigarette boxes of their attractive branding—seems like a no brainer, but in Australia, it looks like the policy caused smokers to switch to cheaper brands and to smoke more. There’s a reading and math program that has done well in India, but as soon as other researchers tried to implement it elsewhere, the effects shrank.

You can always find a one-off study showing that an intervention works, but if we’ve learned anything from the past 20 years of social science, it’s that one-off studies ain’t worth much. It’s so easy to juice your stats and journals are so hungry for positive results that entire literatures can be suspect, and decades of research can culminate in a shrug. “Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t, it depends on all sorts of factors that we can’t really specify, so uh, good luck!”

Even if we take Rossi at his word and there are as-yet-unnamed programs out there that are reliable and effective, the question still remains: why aren’t there more of them? Why do so many of our best-laid plans end up like this:

The answer lies, I think, in a 50-year-old study that is almost certainly false.

One of my favorite genres of psychology experiment is called something like: “the study is probably bullshit but the effect is probably real”. At the top of that heap is The Illusion of Control, a classic from 1975 and a favorite of Psych 101 classes everywhere. Usually, this study gets summarized as “people value their lottery tickets more when you let them pick the numbers vs. when you pick the numbers for them.” It’s as if people think that the mere act of picking imbues their ticket with a bit of juju, which makes them less willing to part with it.

That would be a beautiful study, but it wasn’t the study that was actually conducted. The “lottery tickets” in question were in fact football cards, each one with a picture of a player, their team, etc. Some participants were given the opportunity to choose their football card and some had a card handed to them. Later, just before the drawing, all of the participants were asked how much it would take to buy their card back. On average, the pickers asked for $8.67, while the not-pickers said $1.86.4

I’m sure you can see the obvious and less exciting explanation for these results: when people were given the chance, they picked their favorite players. The people who didn’t get to pick ended up with a card they liked less. This “illusion of control” effect is merely a “reality of people having preferences and acting on them” effect.5

Unsurprisingly, well-powered, preregistered replications with actual lotteries have failed to find any difference in picking vs. not-picking. So that’s that: there’s no such thing as the illusion of control.

Except...obviously there’s an illusion of control! Look around! People will blow on their dice at the craps table, they’ll don their lucky undies when the Knicks go to the finals, they’ll scream “look out!” to the hapless protagonists of a horror movie. When I was a kid, my parents used to send me off to play arcade games without any quarters, knowing that I would simply move the joystick in synchrony with the demo playing on the screen, convincing myself that I was causing the characters to move, when in fact I was merely mirroring them.

Put it this way: why do you think The Secret has sold over 30 million copies? It ain’t the beautiful prose or the sterling scientific evidence. It’s because when Rhonda Byrne tells you that “your thoughts are the primary cause of everything,” it feels kind of true. After all, can’t you jinx yourself by thinking the wrong thing? Haven’t you ever been like “whatever you do, don’t spill this soup” and then the next thing you know you’ve got a shirtful of bisque? And if brainwaves are powerful enough to spill soup, who knows what else they might do!

So no, people don’t believe they can magically improve their chances of winning the lottery by picking the numbers themselves. Still, our intentions feel more potent than they should, and this shows up not only in our harmless superstitions, but also in the way we keep meddling in each other’s lives despite having no idea what we’re doing.6

How do I know my preferred policies will have their intended results? Well, because I intend them. That’s not really my answer to the question; it’s the reason I don’t even think of the question in the first place.

Here’s the real evidence of our illusion of control: we’re so certain our interventions will work that we forget to check whether they do at all.

For instance, the National Science Foundation funds over 1,000 STEM education projects, which are aimed at improving curricula, training, student outcomes, etc. According to an analysis by Stuart Buck, 76% of the time, the researchers running those programs don’t even attempt to evaluate them with actual experiments. Apparently if you have a bright idea about how to teach kindergarteners to code, you don’t need to bother assessing it. It turns out George W. Bush was actually right when he said:

Speaking of the government, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office, many federal programs don’t even define their goals, let alone collect data on their progress toward those goals. For instance, the Department of Homeland Security is supposed to stop people from producing and distributing illicit fentanyl, and so they do things like search people’s cars and walk around with drug-sniffing dogs. When DHS was asked, “How do we know any of this is working? What would success even look like?”, they were like “hmm great questions”. They hadn’t set any goals or collected any data, despite being required to do so by law. As the GAO puts it with characteristic mildness: “As a result, DHS’s ability to fully understand the effectiveness of these efforts is limited.”

Maybe it’s too much to expect that the Department of Homeland Security, especially in its current incarnation, would try to figure out whether it’s doing things that actually work. But it’s certainly not too much to expect of private philanthropists, who choose to give away their money of their own free will. Certainly they would care whether their dollars do anything. Right?

Wrong. In 2018, Kenneth Langone, the Home Depot billionaire, donated $100 million to eliminate tuition fees at New York University’s main medical school. This was supposed to encourage med students to pick lower-paying specialties like pediatrics and primary care, and it was supposed to attract lower-income students to medical school in the first place. But neither of those things happened. The makeup of the student body hasn’t changed, and they’re picking the same specialities they always did.

In this case, it should have been easy to foresee that those beaucoup bucks were going to do bupkis. First, medical school is already a good investment, regardless of income: yes, you take on a big pile of debt, but you also make a much bigger pile of money, even in the lowest-compensated specialties. Second, wiping out that debt does almost nothing to reduce the disparities between specialties: the average orthopedic surgeon earns $564,000 per year, while the average family practitioner earns about $281,000. If both of them work for 30 years, the surgeon earns about $17 million, while the family doc earns about $8 million. Meanwhile, the average medical school debt is about $200k, which is nothing compared to an extra $9 million over the course of your lifetime.

And remember: in this situation, both the surgeon and the family doc attend for free, regardless of how much money they had when they arrived, or how much money they make after they leave. So there’s no reason why free tuition should encourage anybody to do anything differently—except to apply to NYU in the first place. And indeed, applications are up 47%.7

To be clear, giving away dunderheaded donations is better than a lot of things that billionaires could be doing with their money, like buying a second superyacht or digging an additional doomsday bunker so they have a place to summer after the apocalypse. I’m glad that the plutocrats are trying to do something nice. I would just like them to succeed.

When people see our big heap of failed interventions, they tend to go through three stages of grief.

  1. Bargaining

Okay, fine, these high-minded, utopian interventions don’t work, so what we really need is Common Sense and Obviously Good Ideas. For example, if you want to make poor people better off, you should give them money. That’s just Common Sense! That’s an Obviously Good Idea!

Unfortunately, large, well-designed randomized controlled trials keep finding null effects of unconditional cash transfers. In one study, when low-income participants got $2000 with no strings attached, it made them less happy compared to people who got $500 or nothing at all. Psychologically, receiving 20 Benjamins was about 25% as bad as losing your job during the pandemic. That finding might be a fluke, but it also showed up in a study where researchers wiped out a bunch of people’s medical debt and it maybe made them more depressed.

These programs do succeed in sense that when you give people more money, they have more money, and they spend it on things that they need. It’s just surprisingly difficult to find any evidence that having more money makes a difference. (Though note that results are more promising in low- and middle- income countries.)

  1. Denial

This is where people typically raise the no true Scotsman defense: if we get bad results from a good idea, it must be because someone screwed something up, not because the good ideas were actually bad ideas. Maybe the measures were wrong, the implementation was shoddy, or the people who benefitted didn’t fill out the followup survey for some reason.

This response isn’t totally irrational; programs go pear-shaped all the time. Maybe your One Laptop Per Child program only failed because all the laptops got stolen out of the back of the truck. Case in point: in that medical debt study, it seems like 76% of people didn’t even realize their medical debt had been wiped out. (But don’t get too excited: if anything, calling people and informing them of this boon made them slightly more depressed.)

The real problem with no-true-Scotsman-ing these studies is that you must subscribe to the dubious belief that some tiny tweaks will somehow unlock giant effects. This is a holdover from pre-replication-crisis psychology, back when we thought you could, say, subliminally flash an American flag at someone and make them more likely to vote for a Republican two weeks later. It now seems like rinky-dink interventions tend to have rinky-dink effects, or none at all. So yes, we could always pick more appropriate measures, and the facilitators delivering the intervention could always have a bit more pep in their step. That might be enough to make a program slightly more effective, but it’s not enough to turn a null result into a blockbuster.

  1. Acceptance

Acceptance sounds good, but it isn’t. Once we realize how hard it is to improve people’s lives, it’s tempting to believe that doing so is simply impossible, and so we are excused from even trying.

This is a bit like finding out that bloodletting doesn’t work and then concluding that no medicine can ever work. (“Well, We’ve Tried Everything”, Says Society That Has Only Tried One or Two Things.) The social sciences are still in their alchemical stage. We do not understand the fundamental workings of the human mind, let alone what happens when those minds combine in societies and economies. Imagine trying to cure cancer using Galenic medicine or trying to land on the moon using Aristotelian physics—that’s what we’re doing when we roll out programs designed to change human behavior.

That doesn’t mean our ill-informed attempts can never succeed. Both Galen and Aristotle were right about some important things: it was Galen who figured out that urine is produced by the kidneys, rather than the bladder (as was commonly assumed), and it was Aristotle who successfully described how objects move in fluids, even if he attributed it to the wrong forces.

But if we want to solve real, Hydra-headed problems, we need more than a handful of facts. (“Doc, I’m all itchy and covered in spots! What do I do?” “Hmm...did you know that urine is produced in the kidneys?”) Until psychology and its neighboring disciplines grow into scientific maturity, all we can do is guess and check. There’s nothing shameful in that, but there is something shameful in pretending otherwise.

This is hard for us to internalize, because by default we assume that we were born near the end of history. We understand, of course, that we still have a few things to figure out, but emphasis on the few. Just look at our beautiful universities, our begowned scholars, our numerous and inscrutable papers! How can you say we know nothing when we have so many TED talks?

We misunderstand what it feels like to be in the middle of things. Almost no one who read Galen or Aristotle ever thought to themselves, “oh, obviously this is only version 0.1 of our knowledge, all of this is tentative and incomplete, and one day it will be overturned and replaced with something better, something that actually works.” No, they thought to themselves, “Thank u Mr. Aristotle for your many true and useful facts.”

That’s why the worst possible reaction to a failed intervention is resignation. We may not know enough to improve our lot right now, but perhaps we could figure it out, if we tried. Maybe that means another RCT, or maybe it means another century of futzing around in the fundamentals before we can do anything useful.

(This does put a ceiling on the utopia we can expect to achieve in the near future. If you believe that we can perfect human nature by reorganizing society to your specifications, you would do well to remember that, as of now, we can’t even get people to go to the gym.)

That may seem unfair—what a bummer to be born in medias res, when so many of our problems remain unsolved! But if it is an affront, every human before us has been similarly affronted, and some of them chose to begin the work anyway. Whenever we pluck a low-hanging fruit today, it’s only because someone else planted a seed that they never got to harvest. So why should we expect to pluck without planting?

As Seneca put it nearly 2,000 years ago:

I revere the discoveries of wisdom and their discoverers [...] For me those things were acquired, for me they were labored for. [...] Let us make larger what we have received. Let this heritage pass from me to posterity increased.

I know some people don’t feel this way. Some believe that the answers are simple and known and merely need to be enacted by force. Others think the answers are unknowable and will remain so forever. For those folks, I offer an invitation: the next time we conduct the ritual before undertaking some new policy, they may have the honor of playing the part of the goat.

item.title: Google SWE points 48 AI agents at NASA Lidar, finds unmapped Maya pyramid in 72h (890 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://pietromiotti.com/latest/maya-site/?maya, See on Hacker News

5 min read

By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents discovered a Maya site in Mexico that, as far as anyone can tell, no one had reported before. It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive.

Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist.

I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part.

18 October

I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham, the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?"

I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar. From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath.[1]

So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya? Their region is much better covered by public lidar.

That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed.

19 October

I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses.

So how did they do it? They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide.

Me: That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives.

…a few hours later…

Agent: One major village doesn't seem to have been registered.

This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines.

Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir.

And this is what it looks like in 3D.

Me: OK, what should I do?

Agent: You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results.

Me: OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work?

Agent: …instructions for the report… + email addresses

Me: OK, please do the report.

And I went to bed.

20 October

I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one.

The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground.

Then I sent the report to INAH.

21 October

INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location.

To be clear, it's not official yet. But as far as anyone can tell, nobody had put this one on a map before.

So what was it?

This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an aguada, a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses.

I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then:

For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works (Cook et al. 2013) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology (Golden et al. 2016). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way (Auld-Thomas et al. 2024), others used lidar to estimate how many people lived in the Maya lowlands (Estrada-Belli et al. 2025), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces (Šprajc 2026).

What's next

In the report I offered to help with a field check led by INAH. In Mexico, archaeological sites are protected by federal law, and any fieldwork needs INAH's authorisation, so it's now up to the local INAH centre to decide whether to send a team. If they go, I'll post an update.

What I've learned

You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now.

And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute).

At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest.

  1. If you don't know how lidar works, copy and paste this prompt into your favorite AI tool: "Build an HTML page that explains how lidar works, with beautiful visualizations." ↩

item.title: In defense of giving a shit (106 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.possibilityspace.org/blog/posts/in-defence-of-giving-a-shit/, See on Hacker News

In Defence Of Giving A Shit

10/11/2026

A few weeks ago I was one of the judges for the Independent Games Festival. Judging for the IGF is one of the highlights of my year, it's a real joy, but every year there is usually one discussion thread that gets a bit heated. You can normally tell which one it is because it has more comments than all the others - most might have 4-5 comments, but the spicy one will have 15. When I first saw the thread about Big Walk this year, it had 90 comments. I think it had 150 by the end.

Games this year had to have declarations if they used AI. Unlike Steam's current declaration policy, which only requires developers to declare if assets are "consumed by players", the IGF required a declaration for any and all AI use. The upshot of this is that a huge number of games declared their use of AI, including games made by prominent indie developers who have not declared their use in public. The most controversial case was Big Walk, whose developers stated they had used LLMs for "less than 0.1% of the code" to fix errors late in production.

The resulting discussion thread about this included some of the stupidest things I've ever seen anyone write about AI and game development, which truly is saying something. When it blew up today in public, I saw the same arguments being repeated. And I wanted to write this, not to rebut every single argument I've seen, as tempting as it is, but to talk a bit about the actual shape of this problem and what is actually happening. Because what's happening is not unusual, it's not extreme, it's not unfair and it's not a 'public flogging'. What's happening is exactly what is supposed to happen in creative communities. The argument surrounding Big Walk has two parts, so I'm going to break it down that way too: first, should the IGF have a policy on AI content; and second, should House House be disqualified from winning an award. And then I'm gonna ramble and yell a bit and then upload this post and go and lie down in a dark room again.

The IGF Needs an AI Policy

The IGF desperately needs a policy on AI content of some kind, whether that policy is for or against. The problem is that their existing (unwritten) policy was to allow individual judges/jury members to decide on what they wanted to do. I appreciate why you'd have a policy like this, it fits the subjective and personal nature of judging for arts festivals. But the problem is that the AI issue was happening so silently behind the scenes of the IGF that the average indie developer in 2026 is unaware that they are paying money to submit their game to an awards show where 1/3 of the judging pool are immediately going to abstain from considering their game. And I say that as one of those judges, like I'm not in favour of those games being in the IGF, but I think it's unfair to not clarify this massively important part of the judging for an awards show that you have to pay to enter.

But if we agree that it's only fair to add a policy, what should the policy be? For many judges, the idea of banning AI content of any kind - even art - made them mad. Many people were fine with banning it for things like art or music, but felt very strongly that AI code is simply the norm now and shouldn't or can't be banned. The reasons given for this were mostly very stupid, and part of me wanted to list them out here and break them down but I think both of us would lose brain cells in the process that could be lost in a more fun way like playing videogames or running repeatedly into a brick wall. There are so many arguments against this that I truly am losing count of them these days, we have just mostly agreed to ignore them one by one.

What I will say is that these discussions exhibited a lot of really, truly, deeply disingenuous arguments, and I see this more and more now. It was fascinating watching people who know absolutely nothing about AI talking confidently about what it can and can't do, or how it does or doesn't work. In many cases the writer was not even trying to be understood, they were trying to intimidate others into shutting up by wielding scientific/technological language as a way of appearing authoritative. I think this is one of the most hateful things you can do in tech or tech-adjacent spaces. I love science communication, and one of the things that makes me saddest is when people offer up their own stupidity before we've even begun talking about a difficult topic. And the reason they do it is because they spent a lot of their life being spoken to like this, by the worst kind of intellectual bully, and they've concluded that people around them must just understand these issues better.

Of all the arguments against a ban though, there's one I do want to address because I think it gets at the core of "should there be an AI policy", and that's the idea that bans don't work. People pointed out that if you ban AI, how will you enforce it? People can sneak things in any time. And they're absolutely right. How would we have ever known that House House used AI if they hadn't declared it? They could've just snuck it in and it would've taken a significant internal leak for it to ever come out. So maybe banning is pointless?

Here's the thing: when you write down a rule, it doesn't do anything. Rules are not magic. They don't have any power over people. But they do two important things despite this:

  1. They tell everyone outside the community what to expect from that community's space/awards show.

  2. They give everyone inside the community something to point to when a violation happens.

So the rule is both a signal and a justification. It tells everyone what you stand for, and it helps you clearly enforce what you stand for when it matters. This is how it works for PROCJAM too. You cannot enter PROCJAM with generative AI. If I see it, I will delete it. But can you sneak it past me? Of course! You do not need to be very clever to do this. But by having the rule we are saying: look, this is what this community stands for. This is what we will and won't accept. And that creates a sense of community and space. And a lot of people respond to this, because we naturally understand what communities are and what they are for. The same goes for award shows! Many award shows have requirements to meet, and they define what the awards are for and what they believe is important.

The other thing it does is outline consequences.

Although House House could have hidden their use of AI, would they have risked it if there was a rule in place? Probably not. Because the cost of the news coming out is amplified many, many times over if they violated an explicit rule or policy. So it creates a little bit more social pressure as well. Of course people will cheat, but usually they're the kind of people who already don't care. The people who are invested in the community are risking a lot more by doing so.

Bans on the use of AI should not be thought of as shaping reality or controlling what actually happens in spaces. They are about defining and empowering the community around them. This is actually the biggest issue the IGF faces, and the reason the debate was so intense this year: because the IGF no longer has a coherent single community, as evidenced by this issue. It is not really possible for the IGF to continue as it is, because defining a policy will instantly alienate a third of their judges no matter what. But I don't see another way forward, because the competition is currently a chaotic mix of opinions that I think, ultimately, will put people off submitting.

So whatever your position, I think the IGF desperately needs some kind of policy, but pretty much everyone involved is agreed that it doesn't have one now, so we have to address the situation we're in some other way. So:

Should House House Be Given Awards?

Whether or not the IGF should have an AI policy, the fact remains that it does not, so for this year we have to fall back on their current stance which is that individual judges and jurors get to decide for themselves. A lot of games declared AI use in the IGF this year. A few of them would surprise you, but probably none would surprise you more than Big Walk, which is the one that hit the headlines this week. The declaration submitted for Big Walk clarified that LLMs had been used to diagnose and fix some errors towards the end of development, although personally I still find the explanation a little hard to unpack. Regardless, this usage is probably close to the smallest possible amount of AI usage you will ever see in a game. So, what do we do.

The most immediate and obvious problem is that people liked playing Big Walk, and lots of indies know and like House House. If you read the response to the discourse on Bluesky, a lot of the responses boil down to "they are good people" or "they made a good game". I completely understand this response, it's very human and natural, and it's great to hear. If you're suggesting that exceptions should be made for this stuff if we agree the game is good, or if we are friends with the developers, that's also okay but I don't think anyone actually wants to commit to that as a position. How well you know House House should not matter, what should matter is whether you think they made a mistake. Some of the responses that disappointed me the most have made appeals to how good the people involved are, or about how responses to this should respect people's ability to grow or whatever. No-one is disputing any of this. But believing people can change doesn't mean ignoring what they do. House House are a very successful indie studio who have now made two enormous hit games back to back. They know half of the indie games scene, are celebrated the world over, and have sold a lot of games. All that is happening here is that they are possibly being disqualified from winning an award. Once. We need to put this in perspective a bit.

There are a lot of reasons why I think House House made a mistake doing what they did, but one I want to mention here is quite nicely summarised by this post from Simon Roth. Even before the thousands and thousands of layoffs, I knew dozens of freelancers who were desperate to find good work in the games industry. I spend a lot of my days scrabbling around finding little pots of money to fund freelance hires for research, or advising students how to survive in an industry that increasingly doesn't care about programmers. Unless I've misread their situation entirely, House House is not a studio that couldn't afford to hire a specialist for a few days to look into this problem. House House aren't laying off developers to replace them with Claude, and I'm sure they would be firmly against the mere thought of doing this, but we can also clearly see how their actions are part of the same problem. The Venn diagram of people defending this use of LLMs but who would've posted 'QA are gamedevs' in previous discourse cycles is basically a circle, I think, and this is frustrating - you can't just pay lip service to the idea that we're all in this together. It has real meaning for people who are out there watching contracts dissolve as everyone posts about how, well, AI for code is actually a lot more ethical, you see.

It's also pretty clear that House House were aware of exactly what they were doing and how it would be perceived, which to me suggests they don't even particularly agree with the defences of them being posted online. Yes, Valve do not require a public declaration of LLM use, but there are lots of important political stances that House House have taken publicly without being asked to do so. Releasing a statement precisely when there was direct public blow-up from IGF jurors taking a stand to me suggests that they do understand the situation quite well, which does make the lack of earlier disclosures feel a bit less ignoreable. In short, I think House House themselves probably have a more negative read on the situation than most of the people posting about it today. And I think that's cool because hopefully it means they'll figure out what they want to do differently in the future and come out of it feeling better about their process - even if that is "we want to use AI and we're going to tell everyone that".

And this kind of brings me to my other feeling on all this which is how this is being dissected online as some extreme artifact of cancel culture.

Not Caring About Anything Is Good, Actually

The worst takes I have seen on this matter attempt to frame it as an extreme position on the part of the jurors who released the statement, or unfavourably compare this issue with another important issue, or toss around phrases like 'purity test' or therapyspeak. I really feel like we've lost all sense of perspective on AI as an issue. The IGF has no AI policy. It explicitly is asking people to draw their own lines. This group of people drew one. That you disagree with where the line is doesn't make it somehow extremist or unreasonable. We're also talking about an awards show that some notable game designers have been asked to judge for. They are not going to raid House House's offices. Their accounts aren't getting frozen. We're not sending in the feds. In fact, one of the recurring issues with the IGF is that critically acclaimed games sweep the awards and then it doesn't do anything for their success. House House are already a wildly successful company, and they will continue to be in the future - even if they pivoted to using AI for 100% of their code.

It's particularly galling to me that House House are getting the smol bean treatment online when many of the signatories of the jury statement are freelancers who rely on the social network and goodwill with other developers to remain employed and pay rent (in some cases, doing so through coding). These are people who are giving up their anonymity to publicly stake part of their reputation, and by extension their income and survival in the industry, to simply explain how they are approaching their job for the benefit of the community. They could quite easily have done this in silence! This is how creative movements evolve and change. They are doing the hard work of actually addressing difficult shit out in the open, which is what everyone else has been trying to avoid.

Before I wrap up, I wanted to explain one additional thing. I agree with the jurors' statement, but there is one thing I think I differ on to most of them: I don't care about changing anyone's mind any more. I don't say this because I'm proud of it or because I think it's good, I say it because I'm sad and I wish it wasn't the case, but it's where I am. I am deeply tired and truly have no emotional energy for it, and the casual way in which people have normalised and accepted the worst shit imaginable has permanently broken parts of my brain. I've accepted that most people around me are going to increasingly find it okay to use AI, and it is going to creep more and more into their lives and work, and that includes the games industry. I have accepted all this and more. 2026 has seen a surge in normalisation that I simply could not have predicted. I don't think it will be forever, but it will last a long while.

I'm trying to channel the energy I have into supporting spaces where other ways of using, thinking about and making technology can exist. Not to the exclusion of all else, like you can dip in and out of PROCJAM if you want, but while you're in the space you are asked to follow the rules. I think these spaces are useful for lots of reasons, and I think they can be maintained and protected even in the presence of massive societal change everywhere else. I don't think this is the only answer, I just think it's a concrete and specific thing I can and want to do, and have the energy for, and I hope that it complements what other people are doing elsewhere. But often we hear the concern of "you won't change people's minds by being judgemental/hardline/etc" and, with the best will in the world, I am not interested in that any more.

AI uptake is expanding, even if the fate of the AI industry as a whole is unclear. Commentators like Ed Zitron have promised for years that everyone is going to realise they are being lied to soon, and the whole thing will just quietly go away overnight in an economic puff of smoke, but this is not going to happen. The problems that AI is bringing are going to be here for a long time, and any long-term community planning or organisation around this issue has to take that into account. I don't know if the IGF will be one of those spaces that resists AI work. It doesn't have to be, it won't be the end of the world if it's not. But I think it is the time to decide one way or the other, because the current state of affairs doesn't benefit anyone. And then we can move on, and different groups can either rebuild a new space, or redecorate the one they retained.

item.title: Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card (233 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.kate.land/posts/using-voltage-glitching-to-unlock-the-a100/, See on Hacker News

Summary

I’ve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, I’ve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards. Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I haven’t specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG.

Here’s how my “A100-80G” appears and functions.

NVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you more access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIA’s design allows one to relax restrictions by blowing more fuses!

In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. I’ve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here.

Acknowledgements

My work builds on prior research by Jon Pry and numerous others who have dedicated much of their time towards better understanding the GA100 die. I am disclosing my findings subsequent to another security researcher independently discovering the same vulnerability; I believe it to be in the best interest of the public to make this information publicly available. These findings were disclosed to NVIDIA’s product security team ahead of the publication of this article.

GA100 versions

The GA100 is an NVIDIA die that has been used to power almost 20 different SKUs - the A100 being the most well-known variant. I won’t delve into every SKU, but I will present the GA100 manifestations that matter to my work, covering the different versions of the CMP 170HX and the A100.

As fabbed, the GA100 die has 128 SMs, 12 FBPs, 5 NVDEC units, a PCIe Gen4 x16 controller, and depending on the framebuffer size, comes with 4-6 stacks of HBM co-packaged with the die. NVIDIA uses eFuses for yield-control and product segmentation–undifferentiated GA100s turn into more restrictive variants based on defect testing and manufacturer demand.

In one of the most extreme manifestations of product segmentation, the CMP 170HX, an Ethereum mining card with nominally 8 or 10 GB of application-exposed framebuffer capacity, actually comes with, respectively, ~80 and ~40 GB of HBM onboard! This work chiefly centers around how to fully unlock and use that capacity. Previous work has made great strides in unlocking the GA100 via software methods; VFI takes us across the last mile.

Hardware restrictions

So, how does NVIDIA utilize fuses to produce both a datacenter A100 and a mining CMP card from one die? To understand this, we need to take a closer look at the fuse controller located on the GA100.

The fuse controller is a block that contains 16,384 eFuses (512 rows of 32) and a bunch of logic surrounding that raw fuse macro. Its job is to perform fuse readout and programming, protect the underlying fuses, and provide usable “option words” to the rest of the die. These option words subsequently decide how the die functions and what features are enabled.

Each eFuse can be in one of two states (blown=1, unblown=0), and the 512 rows are divided into 4 regions:

  1. Regular fuses (rows 0-221). These are straightforward; often single (pairs of) fuses will map to an option word, such as OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM (an option word that determines whether further fuse programming is allowed or not). Regular fuses have built-in redundancy: for example, OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM consists of a PRI and RED (primary and redundant) fuse, in this case the primary instance is fuse 0 of row 0, and the redundant is fuse 0 of row 1. Some option words are scalars, such as OPT_X_COORDINATE, which is 9 bits wide and ostensibly holds the x-coordinate of the die on the fabbed wafer. Importantly, if a regular fuse is blown, there is basically no remedy to persistently unblow it (save for RIR later).
  2. Fuseless fuses (rows 222-487). This is a weird one. Apparently NVIDIA got frustrated with accidentally blowing regular fuses and ruining their engineering samples, and came up with a system to encode effective option words in a JTAG chain-like format (see this patent). Think about FF as essentially a script that describes what option words should have what values. FF fuses (excuse the RAS syndrome) concern most of the functionality we can unlock using VFI. This is because FF option words can be trivially cleared by simply writing new FF rows! We’ll about this more in depth, later. For now, you should know that NVIDIA also knows this, because under normal conditions, you are strictly prevented from performing any FF fuse blows.
  3. IFF fuses (rows 487-512). These contain instructions in a different format than the FF one. They’re out of scope for this post, and they’re mainly useful for on-the-fly reprogramming of fuse controller option words. They are usually not accessible in a production card.
  4. RIR fuses (8 rows of 32 fuses, which are technically not part of the 512 rows). These are provided by the designer of the fuse macro (TSMC datasheet here) and are essentially the first party designer’s intended “fuse repair” mechanism. The RIR section on a GA100 has space for 16 repair instructions, each overriding the value of an identified single fuse in the main 512 rows. Unfortunately for us, specifically in the 8 GB 170HX SKU, 15 of the 16 RIR words are all ones, and the 16th word encodes a useless repair instruction that can only be rarely leveraged for any interesting unlock. The story is different for the 10 GB SKU, but that’s a matter for another day…

There are two really interesting groups of fuses for the VFI-based unlock:

  1. “Control fuses”. The term comes from NVIDIA’s Tegra hardware headers, they use it to refer specifically to rows 0 and 1, which specify the values of highly security-sensitive option words.
  2. Fuseless fuses, which encode all of the interesting option words that decide whether a GA100 is born to be a measly mining card or an AI datacenter workhorse.

Before we name some of the FF-encoded option words, we’ll have to first understand the FF record format in a bit more detail, then talk about the die blocks that govern the features we are interested in.

Fuseless fuses

Each FF row is a 32-bit record. Bits 0–4 select a chain, bit 5 distinguishes FF from IFF (0 for FF), bits 6–15 select a 16-bit block, and bits 16–31 supply that block’s new value. The JTAG-chain picture from the patent is quite literal here: the controller builds the option data by replaying these records into chains. Fixed locations in each chain correspond to individual option words.

If two records address the same chain and block, the later record wins. For example, 0x0fe805c1 means chain 1, block 23, data 0x0fe8. Appending that record can clear an effective bit set by an earlier FF record. No physical fuse is unblown; a new row replaces the old 16-bit block. This works for FF-backed options, not the regular control fuses in rows 0 and 1.

Now that we know how FF words are encoded, here’s a list of the interesting words and their locations. These were discovered by a particularly helpful researcher who cross-compared FF values and effective option words from different GA100 SKUs in order to differentially understand the FF chain/block to option word mappings, as there is no known official mapping.

The acronyms FBIO/FBPA/FBP/TPC/GPC/PES/ROP all refer to microarchitectural elements, please see this diagram from the GA100 whitepaper to further understand how these are related to each other:

FBP is the internal NVIDIA term for a “framebuffer partition”, with 2 FBPs to one HBM stack. FBPAs are subpartitions, 2 FBPAs to one FBP. PES/ROP are blocks (seemingly graphics-related) that are required for an SM to function.

With this knowledge in hand, what if we could write new FF rows that set the _DISABLE words to be all zeroes, or at least, as permissive as possible given die defects? If we look at how the _DISABLE options are used in conjunction with other elements, we’ll quickly see that these _DISABLE words are the primary lever we have in preventing parts of the die from being “floorswept”. After illuminating the “what-if”, I’ll talk about the “how”: the exact application of voltage fault injection and the fuse controller safeguards we can defeat with VFI.

Floorsweeping

NVIDIA puts these options in charge of setting floorsweep signals, which will render a die element unreachable (and likely powered down). From experiments, I believe the floorsweep lines are specified in RTL, emanating from the fuse controller and terminating in individual functional blocks and controlling some master power/clock domain switch within the block. I have observed the floorsweeping behavior to correspond with very little latency with the value of the fuse controller’s effective status words for each functional block.

Let’s take FBP floorsweeping, for example. On one of my 8 GB cards, OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852: FBPs 1, 4, 6, and 11 were masked. The separate OPT_FBP_DEFECTIVE mask was 0x840, covering 6 and 11. After I reduced the FF-backed disable mask to 0x840 with a replacement FF row, the extra masks on 1 and 4 were gone, but the defective 6 and 11 stayed disabled. That leaves 10 of the die’s 12 FBPs in the effective mask. Functionally, FBPs 1 and 4, which refused register reads and writes when OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852, became responsive after this fuse write.

Although the functional blocks can be “unfloorswept” with FF writes, this does not fully suffice to render the block fully available to an end application - the default framebuffer geometry configuration uses only a portion of each available HBM stack, for example.

To bypass that, we can utilize what is essentially a small modification to cmpunlocker’s method. The usual driver patch for the 8 -> 64 GB unlocks writes to a particular set of feature configuration words (FBPA_CFG, SM_SPEED_SELECT, etc.). The default values are chosen to succeed for the commonly found variant of the 170HX, which has the _DISABLE FF-derived option words preventing certain functional blocks from being used (any attempt to use them will return floorswept errors). With the unlocking FF burns in place, we can write even more permissive words into the configuration registers, resulting in what is functionally an A100-80G.

Achieving the FF burn

With the information we have, it seems straightforward that if one could blow arbitrary FF fuses, any GA100 could be fully unlocked to its maximum capability, as determined by die yield and the populated memory stacks. But how do we blow FF fuses? Let’s take a look at the fuse programming functionality of the fuse controller to understand more.

To request a fuse blow, one must write to the FUSEADDR, FUSEWDATA, and FUSECTRL registers belonging to the fuse controller. Although not nominally accessible to the host or to unprivileged requesters, with the Canary in the Crypto Mine ROP, opening up the responsible privilege level masks is trivial. And so, many researchers have attempted to coerce the fuse controller to blow fuses in the FF region. Some of our shared observations follow:

  1. The fuse controller has an internal FSM, and it indicates its current state via the FUSECTRL_STATE bits.
  2. The fuse controller enters a WRITE_PROGRAM state per each “hot” bit in the requested FUSEWDATA value. This tracks with the expected fuse programming behavior.
  3. However, unless a specific option word is cleared, writes to fuse addresses outside of the FPF range (rows 96-221) do not actually take place. Fuses in this region (believed to be “field programmable fuses” indicating a watermark of which ucode versions have run, alongside other field-relevant information) do take effect, and the fuse controller state machine behaves identically between FPF and non-FPF regions.

The specific option word I am referring to is OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE (“SBFE”), and it is set to be 1 in all production cards. When this option word is clear, fuse programming is allowed in any address. When it is set, only FPF fuses may be blown. To date, no one has found any way to burn FF fuses with SBFE=1, even when operating the fuse controller from HS contexts. It is not clear what “secured burn” truly means, I speculate that there must be a software-only way to perform non-FPF burns even with SBFE=1, and we just don’t know what the “secured” adjective really means here.

Note PLM, HS, ucode, …; I am delving into using a bunch of NVIDIA-specific terminology in this section as the explanation gets deeper. For a really in-depth explanation of what these mean, I refer you to other sources such as Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon.

Importantly, as people have figured out on more permissive cards, it is possible to perform FF burns with SBFE=0! And as it turns out, achieving this state is how we achieve the GA100 unlock. After much trial-and-error, I have resorted to inducing this state via voltage fault injection, and I was able to achieve it. Let’s talk some more about voltage glitching.

Voltage fault injection

Much has been said about VFI, and I’ll leave the in-depth explanation to other sources. In short, applying brief pulses of low supply voltage will often cause unexpected behavior in integrated circuits. I asked GPT-6 Astra to design an STM32G4 based board that taps into the PWMVID signal on the CMP PCB. PWMVID is an NVIDIA standard for voltage regulators, and my glitcher intercepts the PWM signal emitted by the GA100 die, and replaces it with its own waveform fed into the MP2888B VRM driver IC. With my setup, I can induce the card’s own VRM to produce timed glitches for me, which is simpler than MOSFET-based setups and enables faster glitching than attempting to directly drive the PMBus.

The glitcher requires two connections to the PCB, ideally done with magnet/enameled wire. One wire taps NVVDD for voltage sensing, and another wire taps the PWMVID signal. The only other required step for the glitcher to function is the removal of a 0402 0ohm resistor, which will break the connection between the GA100 output PWM pin and the VRM IC. Finding where to place the taps is trivial by tracing the pinout of the MP2888B, specifically its PWMVID and VOSEN pins (the MP2888B shares a footprint with its sibling public chip MP2888A). Test points directly adjacent to the MP2888B enable relatively easy installation of the PWMVID tap.

With this tap in place, a single glitch attempt involves this sequence:

  1. Remove card power
  2. Apply card power
  3. Start a timer (“glitch timer”) as soon as NVVDD crosses a threshold
  4. Execute a proposed voltage waveform by issuing a PWMVID signal, aligned to the glitch timer
  5. Observe card behavior, repeat from step 1 as needed

My setup achieves steps 1/2 with a simple ACPI S0 -> S3 -> S0 transition, which can be done in a few seconds on a modern desktop platform. More intrusive modifications or expensive rigs can probably achieve a better experiment rate, but in my experience this setup suffices to unlock cards in somewhere between 1 hour and 48 hours of glitching time using the approach described later.

For the NVVDD threshold, the Astra-authored firmware uses an STM32 comparator to detect when NVVDD crosses 225mV, after which a tight DMA loop drives the desired duties on the PWMVID pin. After S0, the host inspects the card state and decides what to do next; if it involves another glitch, the glitcher board will be commanded over USB with a glitch pattern. Then the host induces S3 with an RTC timer to wake back up in ~3s (empirically derived period for decent stability).

Sometimes the host will fail to return to S0, I’ve remedied this with relegating bookkeeping and glitch campaign preparation to an SBC (Radxa Cubie A5E) which also can drive the motherboard power/reset button pins via GPIO if the glitch target host is unresponsive.

More specifics are shared in the GA100VFI repository if you’re interested. For now, let’s take a look at the different interesting states we can trigger via VFI, as well as the specific glitch state that we need to burn FF rows. To help illuminate the differences between each glitch state, I have built an empirical model of how the fuse controller starts up when voltage is applied. Note that without the RTL that implements the fuse controller, all we have are guesses. Here are the hypothesized boot stages:

  1. Sense RIR, as required by the fuse macro
  2. Sense (from fuse macro into readout register) control rows
  3. Latch control rows into control row-derived option words
  4. Sense remaining rows
  5. Latch regular fuse values into their option words
  6. Parse FF chain
  7. Latch FF chain values into their option words

These hypothetical stages are based on what I can actually read from the die: controller states, raw rows when CMD_READ works, the published option words, and whether the PRI ring can still reach the rest of the GPU. By looking at a few key values, we can tell glitch outcomes apart. Importantly, glitch patterns and outcomes are very much die-specific, so consider these example waveforms and responses to be just that, examples. Let’s take a look at 3 interesting glitch states.

1. All fuses sensed as zero

Some glitches make almost every published option word read as zero. In one captured state, 669 of 672 named option reads were zero; the other three were error responses. The controller’s CRC status was 0x00 (not parsed yet), the PCIe ID read as 2080 (the base GA100 PCIe product ID, does not correspond to a real retail product), and the GPU’s PRI ring was held in reset.

This state is consistent with a catastrophic failure on behalf of the fuse controller. The card comes up basically unusable, because almost all boot functions are disrupted by the all-zero state. However, interesting enough, the card trains at PCIe Gen4 natively! Some slightly altered variants may showcase sections of fuses being successfully latched, or containing garbled values instead of all-zeroes. I was not able to push any of these states towards an FF burn; in almost all of them the fuse controller is unreachable or dysfunctional.

2. RIR read disrupted

Reading the RIR data on the CMP 170HX 8GB reveals its exact effect: 15 noop repair instructions, and one write that changes the value of a fuse in row 18, whose option word we can monitor. Further, because the RIR sense is consumed internally by the fuse macro instead of directly by the fuse controller, we can observe a disrupted RIR latch by attempting to read the raw row - the observed bitflip remains consistent across the flipped option word as well as the raw fuse row. This sets an interesting chronological checkpoint in investigating die boot (RIR sense must happen prior to other fuse sensing), but is not a useful glitch in itself.

3. Goldilock’s glitch

The successful three-pulse state on my first card seemed to disrupt precisely the row0/1 based option words, while leaving other fuses and option words intact. In this state, all of the row0/1 derived option words are zero. The initial readbacks look like this:

Signal Initial readback
PCI ID and access 20c2; BAR0 and the PRI ring respond
FUSECTRL 0xe0040000 (IDLE)
CRC_STATUS 0x55 (both halves parsed without errors)
DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE 0
OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE 0
ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM 0
FUSECTRL/FUSEOPT privilege masks 0xffffffff for both
Raw rows 0 and 1 Both still 0x53557c3d, unchanged from before the glitch

At this stage, we are still not yet capable of issuing FF writes, because ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0. I am honestly not sure why ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM would ever be zero, given it’s 1 in retail boards, so this almost reads to me like a way to implement a glitch-detection canary (or at least it would be elegant to do so).

Fuse sensing happens one row at a time, with all 32 fuses powered for sensing with one line, meaning it is much more challenging for an attacker to make a single fuse appear as cleared or set. It would make sense, then, to include a “canary” fuse that disables security-critical features (like fuse burning) when it is cleared, because usually the attacker can only manipulate fuse sensing at the row granularity at most. So, when the row0/1 option words come up as all cleared, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0 stops us from burning any fuses.

However, take a look at what we have in this state: DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE=0. This word is normally 1, and it stops us from setting the EN_SW_OVERRIDE register to 1, which then lets us “shadow” most of the option words exposed by the fuse controller. Doing so involves writing to a register CTRL_OPT_*, corresponding to option word OPT_*, which then determines the effective value STATUS_OPT_*. This is what lets us shadow SBFE to be 0. But, even though we have DSOV=0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM turns out to be one of the option words that are impossible to shadow, even with DSOV=0. So it seems we’re stuck.

At least that’s what I thought, and I banged my head against the wall in this state for a while. Then I noticed that there is one fuse controller command I haven’t tried issuing yet: SENSE_CTRL. I had refrained from issuing this, because on the face of it it seems like all of the row0/1 (control fuse) derived option words would match their fused values, which would reset SBFE, turn off software option word shadowing, and leave us unable to fuse. To my surprise, when I issued this command, all of the control-fuse-derived options went to their fused value, except DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE, which remained 0!

With DSOV=0, we can trivially set SBFE to 0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM is 1 because it matches its fused value, and we are off to the races! One wrinkle remains in that FUSEWDATA may have a locked down PLM, but with DSOV=0, we can just write 0 to OPT_SECURE_FUSE_WDATA_WR_SECURE to set the PLM to be all-ones, opening host access for fusing.

At this point, all that’s left to do is to calculate _DISABLE words that match the _DEFECTIVE values for the features we are interested in, and issue FF burns. Note that the occupied FF space and defective bits differ per die, so each burn must be die-tailored.

End results

Framebuffer unlock

On 8 GB cards with 80 GB intact (seems to be around ~90% of 8 GB cards from my limited sample size), the unlock yields the full 80 GB as a usable framebuffer. Multiple synthetic tests (writing pseudorandom words throughout the full framebuffer and reading them back after L2 invalidation) as well as real workloads (such as vLLM and SGLand) are fully functional. As mentioned, one of my cards has only 64 GB intact. In this case, the hardware unlock yields no framebuffer advantage.

Compute unlock

The 170HX is limited to 70 SMs out of the box. In practice, there are almost always >120 SMs non-defective on the die, and the unlock allows using them all. This results in a significant performance uplift, ~1.7x compared to the software-only 170HX unlock, and even an impressive ~1.2x over a retail A100!

PCIe generation

The only thing that stops cmpunlocker from advancing beyond PCIe Gen2 are the FF option words. With relevant bits cleared, Gen3/4 train and are confirmed to be fully functional. When combined with the PCIe decoupling capacitor mod, up to PCIe Gen4 x16 is attainable, matching a retail A100 PCIe variant.

NVLink

Zeroing out the OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE word is only one of the required mods for NVLink to actually work. Because the CMP 170HX PCB is missing the U11 IC (which connects PCIe 3.3v to an NVLink bridge pin), a stock board fails to bring up the reference clock generator on attached NVLink bridges. Simply bridging two of the pins on the footprint of U11 resolves this issue, although it removes whatever regulation or protection was provided by U11. Be careful if you’re bridging GPUs powered by different power supplies, as this will connect the +3.3V rails together unless you leave U11 unpopulated on some of your GPUs! The NVLink bridge works fine if you just patch U11 on one of the boards in the pair.

On the firmware side of NVLink enablement, there is a ROM check that needs to be bypassed with additional host-side commands. I’m sure your clanker can figure it out ;)

While investigating the NVLink unlock, I also found a few interesting quirks with NVIDIA’s NVLink implementation on the GA100. I will be posting a further blog post on this, so stay tuned!

Future directions

With arbitrary fuse burning, we mostly gain feature unlocks. Some security-sensitive options are shipped unblown by default, and burning them may lead to interesting footholds. But what’s more interesting to me are the deeper glitch states where many default-blown security-sensitive fuses sense unblown, enabling routes like debug HS execution, which grant unprecedented access to die internals.

References

  • Jon Pry, A Canary in the Crypto Mine: Defeating Stack Protection in a GPU Secure Coprocessor (2026).
  • Amogh Munikote, cmpunlocker (2026).
  • Otto Bittner et al., The Forgotten Threat of Voltage Glitching: A Case Study on Nvidia Tegra X2 SoCs (2021).
  • NVIDIA, US9230678B2: Integrated circuit having an enhanced fuseless fuse structure (2016).
  • TSMC, TEF07F32X32HD18_PHRM_C180518 electrical fuse datasheet, rev. 120A (2018).
  • hexkyz and SciresM, Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon (2021).
  • TechPowerUp, NVIDIA GA100 GPU specifications.
  • GA100VFI source repository.

  1. Anecdotally, out of the 10 specimens of CMP 170HX 8 GB I have examined, only one has shipped with only 64 GB usable, the rest all have a functional framebuffer size of 80 GB. ↩

  2. Although the Canary in the Crypto Mine paper claims a stable 80 GB on the 10 GB SKU, very few, if any, cards in the wild have been able to achieve this, and solid evidence is scarce. It remains plausible that some number of 10 GB SKUs really do come shipped with 80 GB on-board, however the percentage seems very low according to the community. Most “unstable” 80 GB unlocks are explained with a combination of L2 caching and memory aliasing over a true 40 GB framebuffer. ↩

  3. Enabling NVLink further requires a very small hardware mod due to a missing component on the 170HX PCB, I’ll talk more about this later. ↩

I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15.

It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that.

Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float, because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing.

Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink>) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”.

At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work.

In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort: a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android.

Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs,

–Guido

I wrote this some time ago about Tim:

“”"

I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career.

Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido.

Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them.

Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either.

It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt.

Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot).

When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered.

Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim.

He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so.

Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start.

Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim.

When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on.

It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it.

“”"

In sadness,

. C
